s.en: The night of the partition arrived so quietly it was almost an anticlimax.
No one in the lower ring had been told. The taverns were lively, barges came and went on the canals, and the windows glowed with the same lamplight as ever.
Eleven o'clock.
The warehouse's great doors groaned open to either side.
On the slope down to the canal, the Swallow stood with its wings spread.
Of the patched-up wreck it had been four days ago, there was no trace.
Every last joint had been retightened by Oz's hands, and the canvas wings stretched taut and white in the moonlight.
"I'll go to the boy's boat. Someone's got to mind the little ones."
Oz, toolbox on his shoulder, said it gruffly.
If time stopped, there was no telling what would happen. Sera understood that he wanted, at least, to be with the little ones.
"...Thanks, old man."
"Thank me when you've come back in one piece."
Oz rested his rough hand on Sera's head, just once.
Then, without looking back, he walked off into the mist.
Reinhardt had already gone underground through Old Maintenance Gate No. 7.
Along the roots underground to the tower's base; by air to the top floor. The plan was to close in from above and below at once.
"Right then, here we go. Hold on tight."
From the pilot's seat, Niko hauled the engine's starting lever with all his strength.
The engine coughed twice, three times — then, all at once, let out a roar like a beast.
The propeller spun, and the craft slid down the slope.
The surface of the canal rushed up at them.
"Mr. Niko! Water — that's water!"
"I know! Up, up, UP!"
The wheels skimmed the water and spray hit their faces.
The next moment, their bodies lifted, weightless.
The Swallow flew low along the canal, shot under a bridge, and climbed straight into the night sky.
Cold wind lashed their cheeks without mercy.
Sera clung desperately to the frame of her seat so as not to be thrown off.
Below them the lights of the lower ring spread out like scattered jewels.
"...We're flying."
"Right?! Told you!"
Niko yelled and laughed into the wind.
If he looked close to tears, it probably wasn't just the wind.
Eleven-fifty.
It began along the border between the upper and lower rings.
A membrane of pale blue light rose up from the ground like a curtain.
Exactly the sight from the map in the Council Chamber.
Inside the wall of light, the lower ring's time was visibly slowing.
Factory smoke was all but halting in midair.
The canal's current thickened, slow as honey.
On a bridge, a pedestrian's raised foot took an age to come down.
Niko caught his breath.
On the canal below floated a familiar flat-bottomed barge.
On deck, Oz was looking up at the sky. In his arms, a small figure.
Mina.
Their movements were slowing, slowly, slowly.
"—Hurry!"
Niko threw the stick forward, and the Swallow plunged straight for the Great Clock Tower.
The enormous dial filled their whole field of vision.
The minute and hour hands were closing in on each other at midnight.
"The balcony! Lower left of the dial!"
"I see it! Clench your teeth or you'll bite your tongue!"
Shearing off the balcony railing with a wingtip, the Swallow belly-flopped onto the stone floor.
Sparks flew; wood and canvas tore with a shriek.
When it finally stopped, the three of them had been thrown from the cockpit in a heap.
"...Landing: successful."
"In what sense?!"
The balcony door burst open and two guards rushed out with swords drawn.
Viola swept her fan as she rose.
Violet light flashed — and at once the guards were moving as sluggishly as men wading through water.
"It won't hold long. Let's go!"
The three slipped past the guards and ran into the tower.
Down, down, down the spiral stair that wound through the forest of gears.
With every step, the watch in her breast pocket grew hotter.
Far off, the midnight bells began to ring.
At the bottom of the spiral stair was a heavy iron door.
From beyond it came a low drone.
When Sera pushed the door open, blue light poured out.
The base of the tower: directly beneath the time crystal.
Clinging like a spider to the root of the huge crystal, which reached the ceiling, was a strange machine of black iron.
Countless tubes were driven into the crystal, drawing up the blue light and trembling as though with a pulse.
The time-siphon.
Before it stood two figures.
One was an old man in a black coat. Rector Gregor.
And the other—
"Father..."
Walter Eisen stood before the crystal's pedestal.
The pedestal bore a keyhole shaped like the Eisen crest. In his hand, the key was already gripped.
"Well now. Three guests I don't recall inviting."
The Rector turned and smiled gently.
Exactly the smile he turned on the students from the assembly stage.
"Miss Viola. Did you disobey your father's instructions to come here? What a troublesome young lady."
"Father, you must not turn that key! That man is—"
"Lord Eisen."
The Rector's voice cut across Viola's words.
"Turn the key. Unless the pedestal is opened and the siphon joined to the crystal's core, the partition will not be complete."
Walter's hand had stopped in front of the keyhole.
Viola saw that his fingertips were faintly trembling.
"...Rector. I would ask one thing."
"Yes?"
"Will the lower ring's time truly return one day?"
"But of course."
At that instant, the needle of Instructor Regen's recorder in Sera's hand swung hard.
As though something invisible had warped, softly, all around the Rector.
In the same moment, a low voice came from the darkness on the far side of the room.
"It won't return. Every last drop of the lower ring's time becomes that man's life."
Reinhardt stood at the tunnel's mouth. He no longer wore the mask.
"...Reinhardt."
For the first time, the Rector's smile froze.
"And what is a guard dog that vanished a hundred years ago doing here?"
"Come to sink my teeth into my master's throat."
Walter looked slowly from one to the other.
Then he lowered his eyes to the key in his hand.
"...It was you who ordered me to sell the shards, too. Refuse, you said, and you'd crush House Eisen."
"To protect the family name, I obeyed. Believing that was a head of house's duty, even if my daughter came to despise me."
"But — all because I kept silent, the city's time has been whittled away this far."
Walter drew the key back from the pedestal.
And tossed it to Viola.
"Catch, Viola."
On reflex, Viola caught it in both hands.
"House Eisen guards the Great Clock. From men like you as well, Gregor."
Every trace of expression vanished from the Rector's face.
"Fool."
The old man drew a gold pocket watch from his coat.
The crown was pressed.
The world stopped.
Walter froze, still in the posture of throwing the key.
Niko, Viola, the dust drifting in the air.
Only three people were moving.
Gregor, holding up his gold watch. Reinhardt, his silver one at the ready.
And Sera, a backward heartbeat held against her chest.
"Oh? So Rewinder blood can move even inside stopped time."
The Rector looked at Sera as one might at a rare insect.
"I thought I had torn them out by the roots a century ago. All because I let a single one slip, such a troublesome sprout remains."
"Sera, go!"
Reinhardt pressed in the crown of his silver watch.
In the stopped world, the powers of the two watches collided with a sound like the air itself cracking.
Gregor's time, pushed back by Reinhardt's, wavered slightly.
"I can't hold him long! The pedestal key—"
The key was in Viola's frozen hands.
Sera gently slipped the key out of Viola's fingers.
She slid it into the pedestal's keyhole.
...It wouldn't turn.
Without Eisen blood, it wouldn't open.
But inside stopped time, Viola couldn't move.
— Then just turn back Viola's time alone.
Sera took Viola's hand and pressed it to her own watch.
She twisted the crown backwards, just a fraction.
The frozen violet eyes blinked.
"...Sera? What just—"
"Explain later! Turn the key!"
Viola seemed to grasp the situation in an instant.
She leapt to the pedestal and put her hand to the key.
"In the name of House Eisen — open!"
The key turned, and with a ponderous sound the pedestal opened like a flower.
Inside, the heart of the siphon lay exposed.
A sphere of black iron, ringed by layer upon layer of revolving blue light.
The time-loop: a shell of time that repeats the same moment for ever.
Sera stood before the siphon.
She reached one hand inside the rings of light.
At once, the scene juddered.
When she came to herself she was standing in the same place. In front of the rings. At the very instant of reaching in.
Once more she reached in. The scene juddered. She was dragged back to the same instant.
A third time. A fourth.
However often she tried, she was shut inside the same single second.
So this was the time-loop. A closed second that went neither forward nor back.
Out in the world, Reinhardt's and Gregor's powers must still be clashing.
If he gave out, it would all be over.
Sera clutched her watch.
The second hand was spinning backwards like something possessed.
Turn back time inside the loop, and the shell collapses under its own weight — that's what Reinhardt had said.
But how far back?
Ten seconds wouldn't be enough, she felt. This shell was made of a hundred years of theft.
Sera set her finger on the crown.
And twisted.
Ten seconds.
The rings of light creaked.
Twenty.
The taste of iron spread through the back of her nose.
Thirty.
Her knees nearly went; Sera clenched her teeth, determined not to fall.
Forty. Fifty.
The edges of her vision blurred white.
She could feel the hair falling over her shoulders losing its colour, strand by silken strand.
For every bit of time turned back, her own was whittled away.
She'd known. She'd known, and chosen it.
Sixty.
Just as the strength began to leave the fingers on the crown—
In her hazy vision, someone laid a hand gently over hers.
A warm hand.
A work-coat sleeve. Hair tied back in one.
No answer. An echo? A vision? Or—
But together with Sera's fingers, that hand twisted the crown all the way.
The rings of light shattered.
A sound like breaking glass rang through the whole tower.
Countless cracks raced across the black iron sphere.
The blue light that had been drawn up flowed backwards through the tubes — into the crystal, into the roots, out into the city, all at once.
A hundred years of stolen time.
With a roar, the stopped world started moving.
The gold watch slipped from Gregor's hand.
"—Stop! That's mine — my time!"
The old man's face changed before their eyes.
For an instant the face of an unknown young man surfaced — then a hundred years of age came crashing down upon it.
His beard fell away, deep wrinkles carved into his skin, and his back bent like a withered branch.
Reinhardt readied his silver watch again.
But Gregor was a fraction of a second faster.
With trembling hands the old man grabbed the gold watch from the floor and pressed it to his chest.
"Not yet... It isn't over. If I go back a hundred years, I can start again, as often as I like..."
The gold watch gave off an eerie light.
Gregor's figure shimmered like a heat haze and began to fade.
"Wait!"
Reinhardt lunged, but his fingers closed on empty air.
The Rector was gone.
All that remained was the gold watch's lid, lying on the floor.
The light of the partition faded away.
The smoke of the lower ring began rising into the sky again.
The canal ran again; the man on the bridge set down his foot as though nothing had happened.
On the deck of the barge, Mina's music box picked up its lullaby where it had left off.
The same slightly off-key lullaby as ever.
Still holding Mina, Oz looked up at the Great Clock Tower.
The hands on the dial stood at one minute past midnight.
Sera woke on the cold floor at the base of the tower.
Her head was resting in someone's lap.
"...Sera! Sera, can you hear me?!"
Viola's face, looking down at her, was a mess of tears. Her usual airs had vanished somewhere.
Beside her, Niko was sniffling loudly.
"Idiot... you absolute idiot... making us worry like that..."
"...Sorry."
Trying to smile, Sera noticed her own hair at the edge of her vision.
About half the hair over her shoulders had turned white as snow.
"Oh... this..."
Viola turned her face sharply away, determined not to show any more tears.
"...It suits you. Annoyingly well."
A little way off, Walter sat leaning against the wall.
He looked utterly exhausted. But the eyes he turned on his daughter were gentler than at any time Viola could remember.
Reinhardt knelt beside Sera. In his hand was the lid of the gold watch.
"Gregor escaped. A hundred years back."
"...A hundred years."
"That gold watch was made in imitation of Elise's gate. A shoddy thing that works only once — but enough to carry one man into the past."
"A hundred years ago is an era when he still held power. ...And it's where Elise is."
Sera slowly sat up.
The watch in her breast pocket was quietly ticking, backwards.
A hundred years ago, her mother was fighting alone.
And that man had gone back there.
"Then—"
Sera pushed back her whitened hair.
"I've got to go. A hundred years back."
Viola and Niko exchanged a look.
Then the two of them sighed in unison.
"...I rather thought you'd say that."
"Yeah. Better fix up the Swallow again, then."
Beyond the dial of the Great Clock Tower, the night was slowly beginning to pale.
— End of Part One —
